## What the verse does

==In the name of Allāh, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.== is the sentence the surah opens with, and it opens with a name rather than an argument.

## The name at the head

The verse begins with the name of Allah, and it does so before it says anything about him. That order is the whole of its method, since a book that began with a claim would invite a reader to weigh the claim, and a book that begins with a name invites him to consider whose name it is.

The name itself is not a description. It is a proper name, belonging to one being and to no other, and the verse places it at the head of everything the surah will go on to say.

## The two mercies

Two words follow, and both are built from the same root, which is why the translation renders them as entirely merciful and especially merciful. The first describes a mercy that is vast and unmeasured, and the second describes a mercy that arrives at a particular moment and reaches a particular person.

The pairing is not repetition for emphasis. A mercy that is only vast can feel like weather, and a mercy that is only particular can feel like a favouritism. The verse names both at once, so that the reader is held by something larger than himself and something close enough to reach him.

## Why this comes first

Before a command, before a promise and before a warning, the surah gives the reader two mercies and a name. Everything that follows is placed on that foundation, and a reader who skips the foundation will find the rest of the chapter harsher than it is.

The verse is also said by a person rather than about one. It is the speech of someone beginning, and beginning in the name of another rather than in his own, which is where every act in the surah that follows is meant to start.

## In short

- The name comes before any claim, which is the method of the whole opening.
- The two mercies share a root, so the verse names one quality in two directions rather than two qualities.
- Vast mercy alone can feel like weather and particular mercy alone can feel like favouritism, and the verse gives both.
- The two mercies are placed before every command and warning, and the rest of the chapter rests on them.

## What the verse does

==[All] praise is [due] to Allāh, Lord of the worlds -== makes the surah's first claim, and it makes it as a statement rather than a request.

## Praise and who it belongs to

The sentence says that praise is due to Allah, and the word carries the sense of a debt owed rather than a compliment offered. What is being said is not that a person happens to feel grateful, and it is that praise is owed whether or not anyone pays it.

The little bracket around all is the translation's way of marking a word the Arabic makes absolute. The claim is not that some praise is for him, and it is that no kind of praise falls outside what is owed to him.

## The word behind the translation

The Arabic word is hamd, and it reaches further than thanks. A person thanks another for something done for him, and he praises a thing for what it is. The word here covers both, which is why the sentence can stand at the head of a book that is about to describe a great deal more than gifts.

The difference matters when the reader reaches the hard passages later in the surah. A Lord who is only to be thanked for benefits can be resented the moment a benefit is withheld, and a Lord who is to be praised for what he is cannot.

## Lord of the worlds

The second half of the sentence names him Lord of the worlds, and the plural is unrestricted. Every world there is, seen and unseen, belongs within that ownership, and none is left outside it.

The word for Lord carries both authority and the care that sustains what it rules, so the ownership is not the ownership of a distant proprietor. What the verse has done in one sentence is make an absolute claim about praise and an absolute claim about rule, and the rest of the surah will work out what those two claims mean for a person who has just agreed with them.

## In short

- Praise is stated as a debt owed rather than a feeling offered, which is what the sentence's grammar carries.
- The word for praise is wider than thanks, covering what a thing is as well as what it gives.
- Lord of the worlds is unrestricted, so nothing seen or unseen falls outside it.
- The verse makes two absolute claims in one sentence, and the surah spends its length working them out.

## What the verse does

==The Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful,== repeats the two names of the first verse and gives them a verse of their own.

## Repetition as a signal

The surah has just called him Lord of the worlds, and it now stops to say the two mercies again. The repetition is the argument, since a sentence repeated in a book this careful is a sentence the reader is meant to notice.

What has changed is the placement. The first time the mercies arrived with a name, and this time they arrive directly after the widest claim in the surah, which is that every world belongs to him. A reader who has followed the three verses in order is meant to feel the difference between hearing a name and having a claim about that name tested.

## The distance the verse answers

An ownership that covers every world is a description of enormous distance, and a reader could reasonably feel that a lord of everything is a lord of nobody in particular.

The verse answers that fear before a reader has time to form it. The one whose rule is universal is entirely merciful and especially merciful, and the two words are said again precisely because the claim before them was so large. Greatness is being qualified by mercy rather than standing alone.

## One root, two directions

Both names come from the same root, and the translation preserves the relationship by using the same word twice. The first describes mercy as a quality of the one who has it, and the second describes mercy as an act that reaches its object.

The pairing keeps a reader from two errors at once. A mercy thought of only as a vast attribute can remain comfortably abstract, and a mercy thought of only as a series of gifts can be reduced to whatever the recipient happens to want. The verse gives both, and it gives them in that order.

## In short

- The repetition is deliberate, and its placing right after the universal claim is the reason it is repeated.
- Universal rule could sound like distance, and the verse answers that before the reader forms the objection.
- Both names come from one root, so the verse describes one quality in two directions.
- The order keeps the reader from treating mercy as an abstraction or as a mere supply of gifts, since the attribute is named before the act it produces.
- What the repetition does is hold the largest claim in the surah and the gentlest one in a single breath.

## What the verse does

==Sovereign of the Day of Recompense.== turns the surah from praise to accounting, and it does so without raising its voice.

## The word for sovereign

The translation uses sovereign rather than king, and the choice is worth a moment. A king rules a place and a people, and the word here carries the further sense of holding the whole matter in hand, so that the day in question is not merely under his authority but his property.

The verse attaches that ownership to a day rather than to a country, which is an unusual thing to possess. What is claimed is that the settling of every account belongs to one party and is conducted on his terms, and that no one else has a say in how it runs.

## The day named

The day is named by what happens on it, and the word is the ordinary one for repayment and settlement. It is the vocabulary of a debt cleared rather than of a courtroom, and the difference matters, because a debt is settled by the one who owes it or by someone standing in his place.

The translation has chosen recompense rather than judgment, and the choice keeps the accounting in view. A reader who hears only the word judgment may picture an argument, and a reader who hears recompense pictures a ledger being closed.

## Why it comes here

Three verses have just said that the Lord is entirely merciful and especially merciful, and a reader could stop there and conclude that nothing he does will ever be weighed.

This verse closes that gap without taking the mercy back. The same Lord who is merciful is the one to whom the day belongs, and the surah holds the two claims together rather than letting either cancel the other. Anyone who has watched an injustice go unpunished has wanted such a day, and the verse says the wanting was not naive.

The verse is also the first place the surah asks the reader to hold two things that pull in opposite directions, and the holding is a skill the rest of the chapter will keep exercising.

## In short

- The word translated sovereign carries ownership as well as rule, so the day belongs to him rather than merely being under him.
- Naming a day as a possession is strange on purpose, since what is owned is the settling of every account.
- The word recompense keeps the accounting in view, which the word judgment alone can obscure.
- The verse follows three verses of mercy so that mercy is not mistaken for indifference.

## What the verse does

==It is You we worship and You we ask for help.== is the first sentence in the surah that a person says to God rather than about him.

## The turn in the grammar

Everything before this verse spoke in the third person. He is Lord, he is merciful, the day is his. This verse turns and addresses him directly, and the turn is the hinge of the whole chapter.

The effect is that the reader is no longer listening to a description. He is caught in the act of speaking, and what he finds himself saying is a sentence about worship and a sentence about help.

## The order of the two halves

Worship is named before help is asked for, and the order is not accidental. A person who asks for help does so because the thing matters to him, and the verse establishes what matters before it establishes what is needed.

Both halves are built the same way, with the object placed first. It is you we worship, and it is you we ask for help, and the repetition of that shape is what makes the sentence feel like a pledge rather than a request.

## What the verse excludes

The sentence is exclusive in both directions. What is offered is worship to him alone, and what is sought is help from him alone, and neither half leaves room for a partner.

That exclusion is the answer to a habit the surah will spend a great deal of its length describing. A person is always being pulled toward something that promises to help, and the verse puts the one who is asked for help in the same position as the one who is worshipped, which is the whole of its claim.

The two halves also keep each other honest. Worship without a request becomes a performance that never admits a need, and a request without worship turns the one addressed into a supplier. The verse refuses both on their own, which is why it says them in one breath.

## In short

- The verse turns from speaking about God to speaking to him, and the turn catches the reader mid-sentence.
- Worship is named before help is asked for, because the verse establishes what matters before what is needed.
- Both halves put the object first, which makes the sentence a pledge rather than a request.
- The exclusivity of both halves answers the habit of seeking help elsewhere.
- Worship alone would become a performance, and a request alone would turn the one addressed into a supplier.

## What the verse does

==Guide us to the straight path -== asks for one thing, and it has just said that asking is to be directed to him alone.

## The thing asked for

The request is for guidance, and it is for guidance along a road that is already straight. The word describes something set up and level, without a bend in it that would carry a walker off.

A person asking for that is not asking to be told a direction he could not have guessed. He is asking to be kept on a line, and the difference between receiving a map and staying on a road is the whole of the prayer.

## Why guidance before anything else

The surah has praised, named the mercies and named the day of accounting, and the first thing it asks for is not forgiveness and not provision. It asks to be led.

The placement tells the reader what the chapter considers the primary need. Everything else the surah will ask of him depends on his being on the road at all, and a person who is not on it has nothing to be helped with.

## Asked in the plural

The request is made by a company rather than by a lone speaker, and the form is plural throughout. What is being asked for is a road that others are walking too, so the asking is not a private transaction between one man and his Lord.

That plural shape also carries the reader through the rest of the surah. The commands and warnings that follow are addressed to a people, and this verse has already placed the person praying inside that people before any of them arrives.

There is a further consequence. A road that is walked in company cannot be followed in a way that is entirely private, and a reader who has asked to be guided along it has asked for something that only holds if others are on it too. The prayer is social before it is anything else.

## In short

- The road asked for is already straight, so the request is to be kept on it rather than shown where it is.
- Guidance is asked for before forgiveness or provision, which tells the reader what the chapter thinks he chiefly needs.
- The plural form puts the speaker among a people rather than alone, and the rest of the surah addresses that people.
- The verse turns a prayer into a commitment, since asking to be kept on a road implies walking it.
- Because the asking is plural, the road cannot be followed entirely alone.

## What the verse does

==The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have earned [Your] anger or of those who are astray.== fills in the road the previous verse asked for, and it does so by pointing at people rather than by drawing a map.

## The path and its people

The verse describes the road as the road of a particular group, and that is the surah's answer to a question the reader has just asked. He requested guidance in the abstract, and he is given a company of people who were guided.

The advantage of the answer is that it can be followed rather than merely agreed with. A definition invites an argument, and a group of people asks a different question, which is whose footsteps a person is actually walking in.

## The favour

The first group are those upon whom favour has been bestowed, and the word covers a gift given freely rather than a reward paid out.

What was given to them was guidance itself, and the verse treats that as the greatest thing that could have been placed on them. It also removes any suggestion that they earned the road, since a favour by definition is not owed.

## The two failures

The verse then keeps two failures apart, and the separation is the whole of its precision. One group has earned anger, and the other has gone astray, and the two are not the same condition.

A person who has earned anger knew the road and left it, and the earning is the point, since the word belongs to a wage that is owed. A person who is astray has lost the road without having first found it, and the two are named separately because the remedy for each is different, and because a reader is likely to be one of them without having decided which.

## In short

- The road is identified by the people who walked it, which turns a question of definition into a question of company.
- The favour is a gift rather than a wage, which keeps the guided from thinking they earned the road.
- The two failures are kept apart, since knowing and leaving is not the same as never having found.
- The verse closes the surah by putting three companies in front of the reader and asking, quietly, which of them he is following with his feet.
